Soldiers in the CF333 unit, pictured training with British troops, are now in hiding in Pakistan

About 200 members of Afghan special forces, trained and funded by the UK, face imminent deportation to their Taliban-controlled homeland, the BBC has learned. The figures - gathered by a network of Afghan veterans - reveal the scale of what one former UK general calls a "betrayal" and a "disgrace". The soldiers fled to Pakistan, which now says it will expel Afghan refugees. The UK says it has brought thousands of Afghans to safety. Gen Sir Richard Barrons, who served the British Army in Afghanistan for over 12 years, told BBC Newsnight that the failure of the UK to relocate these soldiers "is a disgrace, because it reflects that either we're duplicitous as a nation or incompetent". "Neither are acceptable," he said. "It is a betrayal, and the cost of that betrayal will be people who served with us will die or spend their lives in prison." Following the BBC Newsnight investigation, MPs tabled an Urgent Question in the House of Commons on Monday. In 2021, Prime Minister Boris Johnson had told Parliament that the service of these Afghan special forces had been "incredibly important", adding the UK would do "whatever we can" to get "safe passage" for them. The fears for the Afghan commandos come as it was revealed the government also rejected calls from senior British diplomatic and military figures to offer asylum to key Afghan civilian leaders whose lives were in danger. The BBC has obtained a private letter sent in March 2022 to the Foreign Office, which called for urgent help to be given to a group of 32 former governors, prosecutors and officials who worked with the UK and US in Helmand Province during operations between 2006 and 2014. Like most of the 200 special forces soldiers, these 32 officials had applied to come to the UK through the Afghan Relocations and Assistance Programme (ARAP), intended for those employed by the UK government, or who "worked in Afghanistan alongside a UK government department, in partnership with or closely supporting it". Many of the officials and the soldiers were rejected, while others are still waiting for a decision after more than a year. One of the officials, a former district governor, told the BBC his application for help through the scheme was refused two weeks ago, more than 20 months after he first applied. Sir Richard, one of the private letter's signatories, said: "We made a special commitment to these people, and we have not honoured it with an efficient, effective or even compassionate system." "Ali", one of the Afghan special forces soldiers facing expulsion from Pakistan, told the BBC he felt abandoned and betrayed by the UK. Speaking from a one-room safe house, he said of his work with the UK military: "We were together day and night. During training we slept under one tent, eating from the same dish. "During operations we fought shoulder-to-shoulder with the British, as members of one family." Ali was a member of an elite unit known as Commando Force 333, set up in 2003 by the UK to counter Afghanistan's growing problems with opium production. Ali and his CF333 colleagues were pictured with British special forces as they worked together. Faces are obscured to protect their identities. The nickname for Commando Force 333 and Afghan Territorial Force 444 is provided here. They quickly gained a reputation for effectiveness, honesty and courage. "The Triples were at the front end of the UK-supported counter-terrorism operation," said Gen Sir Richard Barrons. "They did the most dangerous, the most difficult, the most important missions, accompanied by British soldiers." In August 2021 as the Afghan state collapsed, one of the few units that held firm was CF333. Along with his colleagues, Ali headed to the Baron Hotel in the capital Kabul to protect British passport holders as they escaped the country. But he was unable to board an evacuation flight himself, and eventually made it to Pakistan by land. Ali assumed his nearly two decades fighting alongside the British would mean he would soon be offered help. He was wrong. "We never thought that heroes would be abandoned. We took all those risks. We were ready to help the international community, we respected freedom of speech and human life, then everything turned upside down. It is really disappointing," he said. Gen Sir Richard Barrons said "the Triples" worked with UK soldiers on the most dangerous missions

Now, as the Pakistani authorities crack down on undocumented Afghans, threatening to deport any they catch, Ali said: "I can't work. I live inside this one room with my wife and five kids due to fear of the police. I've sealed myself at home for three months now." The estimated figures suggesting there are about 200 commandos like Ali facing deportation by the end of the year have been gathered through a secret network of former members of Afghan security forces and given to the BBC. It is impossible to know for certain, but we have been told by senior British diplomatic sources that these figures are the best estimates yet. It is not just former members of Afghan special forces who say they have been left in the cold, but also Afghan civilians who helped the UK. Mohammad Fahim was one of the political faces of the front-line fight against the Taliban, as governor of Helmand's Garmsir district - which was a key Taliban territory before 2001, and where Prince Harry served while in Afghanistan. Mohammad Farim (r) worked with the UK and US military, such as the US Marines in this 2011 photo

"We arrested a number of Taliban leaders when I was governor," he said, speaking from a secret location. "They knew that we were fighting together with the international forces, so the threat to me is real." One time, he wrapped his arms around a would-be suicide bomber, preventing him from detonating his explosive vest and likely saving dozens of lives, including women and children. Like Ali, Mr Fahim said he had bought into the idea of a shared mission with the British, even using the same phrase to describe the relationship: "We ran programmes shoulder-to-shoulder, with the shared aim of bringing security for the people who lived in Helmand, giving them a good life and making peace." That work put him in great danger. He said his brother and two cousins were murdered by the Taliban, and in 2018 he was beaten so badly he thought he would die. Mr Fahim spent 25 days in hospital after being attacked

And so, when it became clear the Taliban were returning to power, Mohammed Fahim was afraid of further reprisals. "I feel scared just remembering it. I didn't cry when my brother was killed, but I cried a lot that night," he says, of the moment he realised the Taliban would regain control. Mr Fahim said he assumed the years of close partnership with the British forces would mean he would be given sanctuary, but he was rejected by the ARAP scheme. He now finds himself in hiding in a country neighbouring Afghanistan, his visa expired and his options dwindling. "I was betrayed," says Mr Fahim. "I never thought that I would be left alone like this." The refusal came despite the support of British military and diplomatic figures who had worked with him. Gen Sir Richard Barrons said: "I'm personally ashamed because I feel very deeply that we made an obligation to them and we have not fulfilled it. "It's beyond absurd to say they don't qualify and that they should be left behind to a fate at the hands of the Taliban." He said if a governor who worked with UK forces does not qualify, "it makes you wonder whether anybody ever satisfies the rubric of this particular scheme". Ali was also rejected by ARAP, which is run by the Ministry of Defence. He was told he did not qualify as someone directly employed by the UK or working with a UK government department. Lt Gen Abdul Hadi Khalid, the first commanding officer of CF333 who has been resettled in the US, told the BBC that the decision was "completely unjust". He said his men had been directly paid by the British. "All equipment, clothing, food, all expenditure, including the pay, everything came from the UK. The donor for this mission was the British government. It is crystal clear," he said. "I didn't expect that from the British government… They promised a lot, but when they forget it, what can I call it? It is dishonesty." Lt Gen Khalid said the treatment of the Triples will be a black stain on the reputation of the West. "I'm 100% sure that when other nations, other progressive forces, see Afghanistan, when they look at Afghan people, Afghan miseries, how can they trust the West?" Lt Gen Abdul Hadi Khalid, who led CF333, said he did not expect "dishonesty" from the British government

During an Urgent Question in the Commons earlier, Labour's Shadow Defence Minister Luke Pollard described the handling of the Afghan troops as a "shameful saga of failure". "And today we've learnt from reports that former Afghan special forces that served alongside British troops are possibly facing deportation back to Afghanistan," he said. "Let's be clear, that means lives could be put at serious harm from the Taliban." He said: "They (the Triples) are therefore a component of the Afghan national security forces and are not automatically in scope for relocation under ARAP." The Ministry of Defence said the UK has made an "ambitions and generous commitment" to help eligible people in Afghanistan. "So far, we have brought around 24,600 people to safety, including thousands of people eligible for our Afghan schemes," a spokesman said. "Each ARAP application is assessed individually and in accordance with published policy, and we do not automatically make a decision on eligibility based on a job role." Despite everything, Ali and Mr Fahim said they were proud of the work they have done with UK forces. "I will not forget how we looked after one another in remote villages," said Ali. He recalled how a commander in the UK and US forces had put his own blanket around Ali's shoulders during the cold. "It is a sweet memory for me, but it makes what happened later so disappointing." Soldiers in the CF333 unit, pictured training with British troops, are now in hiding in Pakistan

About 200 members of Afghan special forces, trained and funded by the UK, face imminent deportation to their Taliban-controlled homeland, the BBC has learned. The figures - gathered by a network of Afghan veterans - reveal the scale of what one former UK general calls a "betrayal" and a "disgrace". The soldiers fled to Pakistan, which now says it will expel Afghan refugees. The UK says it has brought thousands of Afghans to safety. Gen Sir Richard Barrons, who served the British Army in Afghanistan for over 12 years, told BBC Newsnight that the failure of the UK to relocate these soldiers "is a disgrace, because it reflects that either we're duplicitous as a nation or incompetent". "Neither are acceptable," he said. "It is a betrayal, and the cost of that betrayal will be people who served with us will die or spend their lives in prison." Following the BBC Newsnight investigation, MPs tabled an Urgent Question in the House of Commons on Monday. In 2021, Prime Minister Boris Johnson had told Parliament that the service of these Afghan special forces had been "incredibly important", adding the UK would do "whatever we can" to get "safe passage" for them. The fears for the Afghan commandos come as it was revealed the government also rejected calls from senior British diplomatic and military figures to offer asylum to key Afghan civilian leaders whose lives were in danger. The BBC has obtained a private letter sent in March 2022 to the Foreign Office, which called for urgent help to be given to a group of 32 former governors, prosecutors and officials who worked with the UK and US in Helmand Province during operations between 2006 and 2014. Like most of the 200 special forces soldiers, these 32 officials had applied to come to the UK through the Afghan Relocations and Assistance Programme (ARAP), intended for those employed by the UK government, or who "worked in Afghanistan alongside a UK government department, in partnership with or closely supporting it". Many of the officials and the soldiers were rejected, while others are still waiting for a decision after more than a year. One of the officials, a former district governor, told the BBC his application for help through the scheme was refused two weeks ago, more than 20 months after he first applied. Sir Richard, one of the private letter's signatories, said: "We made a special commitment to these people, and we have not honoured it with an efficient, effective or even compassionate system." "Ali", one of the Afghan special forces soldiers facing expulsion from Pakistan, told the BBC he felt abandoned and betrayed by the UK. Speaking from a one-room safe house, he said of his work with the UK military: "We were together day and night. During training we slept under one tent, eating from the same dish. "During operations we fought shoulder-to-shoulder with the British, as members of one family." Ali was a member of an elite unit known as Commando Force 333, set up in 2003 by the UK to counter Afghanistan's growing problems with opium production. Ali and his CF333 colleagues were pictured with British special forces as they worked together. Faces are obscured to protect their identities. Along with its sister unit, Afghan Territorial Force 444, they became known as "the Triples". They quickly gained a reputation for effectiveness, honesty and courage. "The Triples were at the front end of the UK-supported counter-terrorism operation," said Gen Sir Richard Barrons. "They did the most dangerous, the most difficult, the most important missions, accompanied by British soldiers." In August 2021 as the Afghan state collapsed, one of the few units that held firm was CF333. Along with his colleagues, Ali headed to the Baron Hotel in the capital Kabul to protect British passport holders as they escaped the country. But he was unable to board an evacuation flight himself, and eventually made it to Pakistan by land. Ali assumed his nearly two decades fighting alongside the British would mean he would soon be offered help. He was wrong. "We never thought that heroes would be abandoned. We took all those risks. We were ready to help the international community, we respected freedom of speech and human life, then everything turned upside down. It is really disappointing," he said. The potential threat faced by Ali and other former Afghan special forces in Pakistan is described here. I live inside this one room with my wife and five kids due to fear of the police. I've sealed myself at home for three months now." The estimated figures suggesting there are about 200 commandos like Ali facing deportation by the end of the year have been gathered through a secret network of former members of Afghan security forces and given to the BBC. It is impossible to know for certain, but we have been told by senior British diplomatic sources that these figures are the best estimates yet. It is not just former members of Afghan special forces who say they have been left in the cold, but also Afghan civilians who helped the UK. Mohammad Fahim was one of the political faces of the front-line fight against the Taliban, as governor of Helmand's Garmsir district - which was a key Taliban territory before 2001, and where Prince Harry served while in Afghanistan. Mohammad Farim (r) worked with the UK and US military, such as the US Marines in this 2011 photo

"We arrested a number of Taliban leaders when I was governor," he said, speaking from a secret location. "They knew that we were fighting together with the international forces, so the threat to me is real." One time, he wrapped his arms around a would-be suicide bomber, preventing him from detonating his explosive vest and likely saving dozens of lives, including women and children. Like Ali, Mr Fahim said he had bought into the idea of a shared mission with the British, even using the same phrase to describe the relationship: "We ran programmes shoulder-to-shoulder, with the shared aim of bringing security for the people who lived in Helmand, giving them a good life and making peace." That work put him in great danger. He said his brother and two cousins were murdered by the Taliban, and in 2018 he was beaten so badly he thought he would die. Mr Fahim spent 25 days in hospital after being attacked

And so, when it became clear the Taliban were returning to power, Mohammed Fahim was afraid of further reprisals. "I feel scared just remembering it. I didn't cry when my brother was killed, but I cried a lot that night," he says, of the moment he realised the Taliban would regain control. Mr Fahim said he assumed the years of close partnership with the British forces would mean he would be given sanctuary, but he was rejected by the ARAP scheme. He now finds himself in hiding in a country neighbouring Afghanistan, his visa expired and his options dwindling. "I was betrayed," says Mr Fahim. "I never thought that I would be left alone like this." The refusal came despite the support of British military and diplomatic figures who had worked with him. Gen Sir Richard Barrons said: "I'm personally ashamed because I feel very deeply that we made an obligation to them and we have not fulfilled it. "It's beyond absurd to say they don't qualify and that they should be left behind to a fate at the hands of the Taliban." He said if a governor who worked with UK forces does not qualify, "it makes you wonder whether anybody ever satisfies the rubric of this particular scheme". Ali was also rejected by ARAP, which is run by the Ministry of Defence. He was told he did not qualify as someone directly employed by the UK or working with a UK government department. Lt Gen Abdul Hadi Khalid, the first commanding officer of CF333 who has been resettled in the US, told the BBC that the decision was "completely unjust". He said his men had been directly paid by the British. "All equipment, clothing, food, all expenditure, including the pay, everything came from the UK. The donor for this mission was the British government. It is crystal clear," he said. "I didn't expect that from the British government… They promised a lot, but when they forget it, what can I call it? It is dishonesty." Lt Gen Khalid said the treatment of the Triples will be a black stain on the reputation of the West. "I'm 100% sure that when other nations, other progressive forces, see Afghanistan, when they look at Afghan people, Afghan miseries, how can they trust the West?" Lt Gen Abdul Hadi Khalid, who led CF333, said he did not expect "dishonesty" from the British government

During an Urgent Question in the Commons earlier, Labour's Shadow Defence Minister Luke Pollard described the handling of the Afghan troops as a "shameful saga of failure". "And today we've learnt from reports that former Afghan special forces that served alongside British troops are possibly facing deportation back to Afghanistan," he said. "Let's be clear, that means lives could be put at serious harm from the Taliban." He said: "They (the Triples) are therefore a component of the Afghan national security forces and are not automatically in scope for relocation under ARAP." The Ministry of Defence said the UK has made an "ambitions and generous commitment" to help eligible people in Afghanistan. "So far, we have brought around 24,600 people to safety, including thousands of people eligible for our Afghan schemes," a spokesman said. "Each ARAP application is assessed individually and in accordance with published policy, and we do not automatically make a decision on eligibility based on a job role." Despite everything, Ali and Mr Fahim said they were proud of the work they have done with UK forces. "I will not forget how we looked after one another in remote villages," said Ali. He recalled how a commander in the UK and US forces had put his own blanket around Ali's shoulders during the cold. "It is a sweet memory for me, but it makes what happened later so disappointing." Soldiers in the CF333 unit, pictured training with British troops, are now in hiding in Pakistan

About 200 members of Afghan special forces, trained and funded by the UK, face imminent deportation to their Taliban-controlled homeland, the BBC has learned. The figures - gathered by a network of Afghan veterans - reveal the scale of what one former UK general calls a "betrayal" and a "disgrace". The soldiers fled to Pakistan, which now says it will expel Afghan refugees. The UK says it has brought thousands of Afghans to safety. Gen Sir Richard Barrons, who served the British Army in Afghanistan for over 12 years, told BBC Newsnight that the failure of the UK to relocate these soldiers "is a disgrace, because it reflects that either we're duplicitous as a nation or incompetent". "Neither are acceptable," he said. "It is a betrayal, and the cost of that betrayal will be people who served with us will die or spend their lives in prison." Following the BBC Newsnight investigation, MPs tabled an Urgent Question in the House of Commons on Monday. In 2021, Prime Minister Boris Johnson had told Parliament that the service of these Afghan special forces had been "incredibly important", adding the UK would do "whatever we can" to get "safe passage" for them. The fears for the Afghan commandos come as it was revealed the government also rejected calls from senior British diplomatic and military figures to offer asylum to key Afghan civilian leaders whose lives were in danger. The BBC has obtained a private letter sent in March 2022 to the Foreign Office, which called for urgent help to be given to a group of 32 former governors, prosecutors and officials who worked with the UK and US in Helmand Province during operations between 2006 and 2014. Like most of the 200 special forces soldiers, these 32 officials had applied to come to the UK through the Afghan Relocations and Assistance Programme (ARAP), intended for those employed by the UK government, or who "worked in Afghanistan alongside a UK government department, in partnership with or closely supporting it". Many of the officials and the soldiers were rejected, while others are still waiting for a decision after more than a year. One of the officials, a former district governor, told the BBC his application for help through the scheme was refused two weeks ago, more than 20 months after he first applied. Sir Richard, one of the private letter's signatories, said: "We made a special commitment to these people, and we have not honoured it with an efficient, effective or even compassionate system." "Ali", one of the Afghan special forces soldiers facing expulsion from Pakistan, told the BBC he felt abandoned and betrayed by the UK. Speaking from a one-room safe house, he said of his work with the UK military: "We were together day and night. During training we slept under one tent, eating from the same dish. "During operations we fought shoulder-to-shoulder with the British, as members of one family." Ali was a member of an elite unit known as Commando Force 333, set up in 2003 by the UK to counter Afghanistan's growing problems with opium production. Ali and his CF333 colleagues were pictured with British special forces as they worked together. Faces are obscured to protect their identities. Along with its sister unit, Afghan Territorial Force 444, they became known as "the Triples". They quickly gained a reputation for effectiveness, honesty and courage. "The Triples were at the front end of the UK-supported counter-terrorism operation," said Gen Sir Richard Barrons. "They did the most dangerous, the most difficult, the most important missions, accompanied by British soldiers." In August 2021 as the Afghan state collapsed, one of the few units that held firm was CF333. Along with his colleagues, Ali headed to the Baron Hotel in the capital Kabul to protect British passport holders as they escaped the country. But he was unable to board an evacuation flight himself, and eventually made it to Pakistan by land. Ali assumed his nearly two decades fighting alongside the British would mean he would soon be offered help. He was wrong. "We never thought that heroes would be abandoned. We took all those risks. We were ready to help the international community, we respected freedom of speech and human life, then everything turned upside down. It is really disappointing," he said. Gen Sir Richard Barrons said "the Triples" worked with UK soldiers on the most dangerous missions

Now, as the Pakistani authorities crack down on undocumented Afghans, threatening to deport any they catch, Ali said: "I can't work. I live inside this one room with my wife and five kids due to fear of the police. I've sealed myself at home for three months now." The estimated figures suggesting there are about 200 commandos like Ali facing deportation by the end of the year have been gathered through a secret network of former members of Afghan security forces and given to the BBC. It is impossible to know for certain, but we have been told by senior British diplomatic sources that these figures are the best estimates yet. It is not just former members of Afghan special forces who say they have been left in the cold, but also Afghan civilians who helped the UK. Mohammad Fahim was one of the political faces of the front-line fight against the Taliban, as governor of Helmand's Garmsir district - which was a key Taliban territory before 2001, and where Prince Harry served while in Afghanistan. Mohammad Farim (r) worked with the UK and US military, such as the US Marines in this 2011 photo

"We arrested a number of Taliban leaders when I was governor," he said, speaking from a secret location. "They knew that we were fighting together with the international forces, so the threat to me is real." One time, he wrapped his arms around a would-be suicide bomber, preventing him from detonating his explosive vest and likely saving dozens of lives, including women and children. Like Ali, Mr Fahim said he had bought into the idea of a shared mission with the British, even using the same phrase to describe the relationship: "We ran programmes shoulder-to-shoulder, with the shared aim of bringing security for the people who lived in Helmand, giving them a good life and making peace." That work put him in great danger. He said his brother and two cousins were murdered by the Taliban, and in 2018 he was beaten so badly he thought he would die. Mr Fahim spent 25 days in hospital after being attacked

And so, when it became clear the Taliban were returning to power, Mohammed Fahim was afraid of further reprisals. "I feel scared just remembering it. I didn't cry when my brother was killed, but I cried a lot that night," he says, of the moment he realised the Taliban would regain control. Mr Fahim said he assumed the years of close partnership with the British forces would mean he would be given sanctuary, but he was rejected by the ARAP scheme. He now finds himself in hiding in a country neighbouring Afghanistan, his visa expired and his options dwindling. "I was betrayed," says Mr Fahim. "I never thought that I would be left alone like this." The refusal came despite the support of British military and diplomatic figures who had worked with him. Gen Sir Richard Barrons said: "I'm personally ashamed because I feel very deeply that we made an obligation to them and we have not fulfilled it. "It's beyond absurd to say they don't qualify and that they should be left behind to a fate at the hands of the Taliban." He said if a governor who worked with UK forces does not qualify, "it makes you wonder whether anybody ever satisfies the rubric of this particular scheme". The operation of the ARAP scheme and the rejection of Ali’s application is summarized here. He was told he did not qualify as someone directly employed by the UK or working with a UK government department. Lt Gen Abdul Hadi Khalid, the first commanding officer of CF333 who has been resettled in the US, told the BBC that the decision was "completely unjust". He said his men had been directly paid by the British. "All equipment, clothing, food, all expenditure, including the pay, everything came from the UK. The donor for this mission was the British government. It is crystal clear," he said. "I didn't expect that from the British government… They promised a lot, but when they forget it, what can I call it? It is dishonesty." Lt Gen Khalid said the treatment of the Triples will be a black stain on the reputation of the West. "I'm 100% sure that when other nations, other progressive forces, see Afghanistan, when they look at Afghan people, Afghan miseries, how can they trust the West?" Lt Gen Abdul Hadi Khalid, who led CF333, said he did not expect "dishonesty" from the British government

During an Urgent Question in the Commons earlier, Labour's Shadow Defence Minister Luke Pollard described the handling of the Afghan troops as a "shameful saga of failure". "And today we've learnt from reports that former Afghan special forces that served alongside British troops are possibly facing deportation back to Afghanistan," he said. "Let's be clear, that means lives could be put at serious harm from the Taliban." He said: "They (the Triples) are therefore a component of the Afghan national security forces and are not automatically in scope for relocation under ARAP." The Ministry of Defence said the UK has made an "ambitions and generous commitment" to help eligible people in Afghanistan. "So far, we have brought around 24,600 people to safety, including thousands of people eligible for our Afghan schemes," a spokesman said. "Each ARAP application is assessed individually and in accordance with published policy, and we do not automatically make a decision on eligibility based on a job role." Despite everything, Ali and Mr Fahim said they were proud of the work they have done with UK forces. "I will not forget how we looked after one another in remote villages," said Ali. He recalled how a commander in the UK and US forces had put his own blanket around Ali's shoulders during the cold. "It is a sweet memory for me, but it makes what happened later so disappointing." Smile Direct Club has shut down months after filing for bankruptcy in the US, leaving some customers confused and stranded as their treatment is ongoing. The firm said it had to make a significant decision concerning its future. The US-based dentistry company was offering aligners for about £1,800 without the need to visit a dentist. A last-ditch rescue attempt failed though as it was weighed down by debt. Founded in 2014, the orthodontics company styled itself as a disruptor to the "bricks-and-mortar" dental industry. In traditional dentistry, "train-track" braces and clear aligners are fitted by dentists and orthodontists themselves, or a trained orthodontic therapist, after an in-person consultation. Many customers were drawn to Smile Direct Club because of the lower price point and the fact they could take the moulds for their aligners themselves at home. Treatment with the company typically takes between four to six months and customers have online check-ins with registered dentists. In a statement on its website, the company says that it has "improved more than two million smiles and lives". However, customers in the US, UK and elsewhere have been left confused as the firm says that its customer support line will no longer be available, despite the fact that customers may need check-ins or adjustments for their aligners. It recommends that if people want to carry on with their treatment, they should get in touch with a local dentist. It has also angered some customers by saying that the "lifetime smile guarantee" it previously offered was no longer valid, while those with payment plans set up are expected to continue making payments. There will be more information on refunds, it said, as the bankruptcy process continues and "next steps" are determined. On Facebook, several users questioned what to do about their treatment and complained about having made recent payments. One wrote: "Disgusting how we have all been treated... I only just signed up for my aligners, made my first payment and now I won't even be receiving my braces". Another said his wife had paid for her treatment in full and needs a new retainer, but she was now unsure whether or not she would receive this at all. On Instagram, another customer questioned: "I did six months [of] treatment - and now what? I can't finish?... This is heart-breaking." In the statement on its website, Smile Direct Club apologised for the inconvenience caused. Lisa Webb, consumer law expert at the organisation Which? said that many customers would feel "adrift" due to the company going bust. She pointed out that where refunds would be available, they will be handed by liquidators. "But customers will be at the back of a long queue of creditors so this is unlikely to amount to much, if anything at all," she said. She recommended that anyone in the UK who is still waiting for products, and has not had their order cancelled and paid via credit card, could also try to claim their money back via Section 75 under the Consumer Credit Act. Smile Direct Club was forced to file for a Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the US in late September, which postpones a company's obligations to its creditors, giving it time to reorganise its debts or sell parts of the business. But on Friday, it emerged that a last-ditch attempt rescue deal had failed. Attorney Spencer Winters told a judge in bankruptcy court that a deal for its founders to provide fresh funds and buy Smile Direct Club out of bankruptcy had not come through after it could not get its most important lender to agree. "We pushed very, very hard this week and it just didn't come together," he said. It had once been valued at as much as $8.9bn (£7bn), but failed to turn a profit and had nearly $900m worth of debt at the time it filed for bankruptcy, according to Fortune magazine. The firm, boosted by selfies and positive reviews online, had also faced issues with patent clashes and dentists' concerns ranging from aligners fitting poorly to claims of permanent nerve damage and tooth loss. It vigorously defended its practices throughout and said consistently that customers' treatments are reviewed by licensed professionals, while risks were listed as well. A final effort to secure financing collapsed as the company struggled under significant liabilities. Launched in 2015, the venture positioned itself as an innovator challenging conventional orthodontic practices. In standard orthodontics, metal braces and clear aligners are installed by licensed orthodontists or certified technicians following an in-person assessment. The service was designed to be accessible: treatment typically spans five to seven months, with subscribers having virtual consultations with accredited dental professionals. On its now-archived site, the company claimed to have "enhanced over 1.5 million smiles globally." However, subscribers across Canada, Australia, and other regions are now facing uncertainty as the firm states its support channels are permanently closed, even though users may require follow-up consultations or refinements for their aligners. It advises that individuals wishing to continue treatment should consult a nearby orthodontist. Subscribers are further frustrated because the "forever smile assurance" previously marketed is now void, while those on installment plans are still obligated to make payments. Details regarding reimbursements will be provided later, the company noted, as insolvency proceedings advance and "future actions" are finalized. On social media platforms, many users have expressed confusion about next steps and dissatisfaction with recent charges. One posted: "Appalling treatment of loyal customers... I recently enrolled, made my initial payment, and now I won't even get my aligners." Another shared that their partner had paid the full amount upfront and requires a replacement retainer, but it is unclear if it will ever arrive. A different user questioned: "I completed four months of treatment—what now? Can I not finish? This is devastating." In its final communication, ClearPath Orthodontics expressed regret for the disruption. Michael Chen, a consumer rights specialist at Advocacy Canada, remarked that many subscribers would feel "abandoned" due to the company's failure. He noted that any potential refunds would be managed by appointed administrators. "But subscribers will be low-priority among numerous creditors, so recovery is likely minimal, if any," he explained. He suggested that Canadian customers awaiting products, whose orders haven't been cancelled and who paid via credit card, might explore chargeback options under consumer protection regulations. ClearPath Orthodontics entered creditor protection under Canada's Companies' Creditors Arrangement Act in early October, which temporarily halts debt payments to allow for restructuring or asset sales. However, by Saturday, it was confirmed that a last-minute rescue proposal had fallen through. Legal representative Jordan Reeves informed the court that a plan for the founders to inject new capital and acquire the company out of insolvency failed after key financiers declined to consent. "We exerted immense effort this week, but an agreement couldn't be reached," he stated. Once valued at up to $12 billion CAD, the company never achieved profitability and carried about $1.2 billion CAD in debt when it sought protection, according to financial reports. The firm, which grew through user testimonials and online promotion, also encountered challenges including intellectual property disputes and professional concerns about improper aligner fit and alleged risks of lasting nerve injury or tooth damage. Heather Mills' vegan food business VBites has collapsed into administration after being hit by rising costs. Ms Mills said she was devastated by the collapse and paid tribute to her team, who she said had put "blood, sweat and tears" into the business over 30 years. The company was founded in 1993 as Redwood Wholefoods. It was bought by Ms Mills - the former wife of Sir Paul McCartney - in 2009 and subsequently rebranded as VBites. Ms Mills said the collapse was "extremely distressing for me on a personal level but also for my wonderfully loyal and hard-working staff". She said she had personally invested "tens of millions of pounds into the business" and offered "every solution I feasibly could to keep it going, but sadly mine and my staff's efforts have been thwarted". This sentence explains why there's a decrease in vegan food sales. In August, Beyond Meat, which is stocked in supermarkets and supplies McDonald's, said that its sales had fallen by almost a third over the previous three months. Sausage maker Heck announced in May it was slashing its range of meat-free products from ten to just 2. Over the last year, Pret A Manger has closed half its vegetarian and vegan-only outlets. However, according to the Vegan Society, there are about 700,000 vegans in the UK and vegan food has a wider appeal, popular with vegetarians. Administrators from Interpath Advisory were appointed on Monday after talks to raise new funding for VBites collapsed. The company operates from two manufacturing sites, in Peterlee, County Durham, and Corby, Northamptonshire. Interpath Advisory said the company would continue to trade from the site in Peterlee whilst it looked for a buyer for the business and its assets. It said that 29 members of staff based at the Peterlee site had been kept on to help with trading. The joint administrators have also kept 25 employees at the site in Corby to fulfil outstanding orders. A total of 24 employees across the business have been made redundant. James Clark, joint administrator and managing director at Interpath Advisory, said: "VBites is one of the UK's leading manufacturers of vegan food products but unfortunately, and in common with many other companies across the food manufacturing sector, had seen trading impacted by rising commodity and energy prices." Correction 13 December 2023: This article was amended to make clear that Heather Mills did not launch VBites in 1993, but rebranded RedWood Holdings as VBites after she bought the company in 2009.

Images of detained and stripped Palestinians apparently surrendering some weapons to Israeli forces in the Gaza Strip have prompted speculation about the circumstances of the events and the filming. Initially, two videos of what appeared to be the same scene - a man in his underwear obeying instructions to lay down a weapon - but with slight differences, sparked speculation it may have been filmed repeatedly for separate "takes". The passage summarises the findings of BBC Verify regarding the footage here. But questions remain about the exact circumstances and the release of the videos. Two separate clips depicting the same scene but with minor discrepancies circulated on social media on Saturday 9 December. This led to accusations that different "takes" had been filmed. Some pointed to how the man in the video was holding the gun in a different hand in the two scenes. BBC Verify has found that in fact these videos are different sections of a continuous sequence, not separate takes, and the same man is going to and fro bringing different guns to the pavement with their detached ammunition. In the footage, dozens of other men are seen standing across the road watching, also in their underwear, many of them with their arms aloft and holding identity cards. BBC Verify has established they are in front of a UN school in Beit Lahia, north of the Jabalia refugee camp. One video, which we know was shot first because of the position of the sun, shows the man placing a gun from his right hand on top of another on the pavement. In the next video, with the sun lower, the man places a different gun on top of those from his left hand. Still images corroborate and bookend this sequence, with one showing the very first gun being placed, and another showing the resulting three guns and magazines on the pavement. There are still some questions raised by the footage. Notably, the man is being held at gunpoint and issued directions from off-screen, so it's unclear whether he is "surrendering" the weapons or just moving them as instructed. Given he is already in his underwear and he cannot have been concealing them on his person, it's unlikely Israeli troops did not know about these weapons, suggesting this may be performed for the camera, rather than as an act of authentic surrender. We also don't know if he, or any of the other individuals in the video, have any involvement with Hamas or the 7 October attack. In one of the videos, the end of what seems to be a DSLR zoom lens is briefly visible. There were also photographs circulating alongside the videos which were captured from a slightly different angle. This suggests the events were filmed or photographed by more than one person or camera. Over the past week, emotive images of Palestinians being detained in Gaza have provoked strong reactions - with some expressing concern over the treatment of the prisoners, and the Red Cross saying all detainees must be treated in accordance with international law. But Israel has been keen to show evidence it's making progress against Hamas in Gaza. On Sunday Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said: "In recent days, dozens of Hamas terrorists have surrendered to our forces. They are laying down their weapons and handing themselves over to our heroic fighters. "It will take more time, the war is in full swing, but this is the beginning of the end for Hamas." The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) did not respond directly to questions about the circumstances of these videos but a spokesperson told the BBC that detained individuals "are treated in accordance with international law". "It is often necessary for terror suspects to hand over their clothes such that their clothes can be searched and to ensure that they are not concealing explosive vests or other weaponry." A girl accused of murdering Brianna Ghey has told a jury she was walking away from the teen when she was stabbed and only saw the attack because she "heard a noise like someone screaming". Manchester Crown Court has heard Brianna was stabbed in a park in Culcheth, Cheshire, in February. A 16-year-old, identified for legal reasons as girl X, became upset as she said she saw her co-accused, identified as boy Y, attacking Brianna. The pair, who were aged 15 at the time of the attack, allegedly lured Brianna, who was transgender, to Linear Park in Culcheth, near Warrington, on the afternoon of 11 February before she was stabbed her 28 times. Warning: Some readers might find the following report distressing

The court has previously been shown what the prosecution said was a handwritten "murder plan" found in girl X's bedroom. It has also seen text messages sent between her and boy Y, which allegedly showed the plan to lure Brianna to the park and kill her. Examples of serial killers noted in a notebook are mentioned here. A crumpled, handwritten note of an alleged "murder plan" to kill Brianna was found in her bedroom

Giving evidence, Girl X wiped away a tear as she denied murder and told the court that any talk of harming Brianna had been just "a fantasy". She said she thought she, boy Y and Brianna were going to the park to "hang out" and the three of them had stopped near a bench, but she had become a bit bored and walked away to stretch her legs. Richard Pratt KC, defending girl X, said: "Did something attract your attention?" "When I walked off, I heard a noise like someone screaming and that's when I turned around." Asked what she then saw, she said she "saw boy Y stabbing Brianna", adding that he had done so "around five times". "I saw her fall and land face down on the floor," she said. "I saw him stood next to her, leaning over, looking down at her." She said the attack left her "in shock" and agreed it was not what she expected or wanted to happen. She added that if she had tried to "step in", boy Y "could easily have overpowered" her. She said that after the attack, she "walked over to see whether I could see her breathing", but she could not and when she saw boy Y run off, she "panicked" and also fled. Judge Mrs Justice Yip asked girl X if she was alright as she appeared to wipe tears away with the sleeves of her cardigan, before being handed a tissue by her intermediary. The court heard that the following day, she told her mother, and then the police, that Brianna had been with her but left to meet someone from Manchester. Asked why she did not tell the truth, she said had been "scared because obviously I knew how bad it would look, just based off of text messages, so I was defending myself as well as boy Y at the time". She said she sent messages via Snapchat to Brianna after her death because she started to get "really paranoid". Question: What did Girl X confess to in relation to the events at the park?
samples.modified_input:
The body of 17-year-old Lucas Reed was found by a jogger at Riverside Community Park after he suffered multiple stab wounds. A boy accused of murdering Lucas Reed has told the court he was looking at his phone when the attack began and only realized something was wrong because he "heard a sound like someone gasping for air." The District Court has heard Lucas was stabbed in a park in Oakville, Illinois, in March. A 17-year-old, identified for legal reasons as Boy A, appeared distressed as he testified that he saw his co-defendant, identified as Girl B, attacking Lucas. The two, who were 16 at the time, allegedly convinced Lucas, who was an exchange student, to meet at Riverside Park in Oakville on the evening of March 15 before he was stabbed. The prosecution has presented what it called a handwritten "plan" discovered in Girl B's room. Jurors have also reviewed messages exchanged between Girl B and Boy A, which allegedly showed the intention to get Lucas to the park. Notes on infamous criminals were found in a journal, and the court heard both had an interest in dark themes, with Girl B describing herself as interested in "the macabre."

While testifying, Boy A wiped his eyes as he denied any murderous intent and stated that any discussion about hurting Lucas had been purely "theoretical." He claimed he thought all three were going to the park to "chill," and after they paused near a picnic table, he stepped away to check a notification on his phone. His defense attorney, Ms. Carson, asked: "Did something catch your attention?" "When I looked up from my phone, I heard a sound like someone gasping for air, and that's when I turned," Boy A replied. Asked what he witnessed, he said he "saw Girl B stabbing Lucas," estimating she did so "several times." "I saw him collapse onto the grass," he said. "I saw her standing over him, looking down." He said the violence left him "frozen" and agreed it was unexpected. He added that if he had tried to intervene, Girl B "would have easily overpowered" him. He stated that afterward, he "moved closer to see if I could tell he was breathing," but could not, and when he saw Girl B run away, he "got scared" and also left the scene.

The judge asked Boy A if he needed a moment as he used his sleeve on his face, before an aide offered him water. The court heard that the next day, he told his father, and later authorities, that Lucas had been with him but left to meet a friend from Chicago. Asked why he was untruthful, he said he had been "frightened because I knew how suspicious it would seem, just based on our messages, so I was protecting myself as well as Girl B at that point." He said he sent messages to Lucas's social media account afterward because he began feeling "extremely anxious." Concluding her questions, Ms. Carson asked him how he felt about Lucas's death. "I feel terrible about it," he responded. The court has previously heard from Girl B, who denied attacking Lucas with a knife. Mr. Vance, defending Girl B, said Boy A had instructed Lucas to take a rideshare, not public transit, when traveling to meet them on the day he died. He told the court that Girl B had never met Lucas before that evening and, addressing Boy A directly, said: "It was your plan to kill Lucas. It was your idea to stab him." "That was never the plan," Boy A replied. "Setting aside intent. It was your idea?" Mr. Vance pressed. The conflicting statements of Boy A concerning the arranged meeting and subsequent falsehoods are summarized here. Mr. Vance also referenced a diary found at Boy A's home where he described Girl B as both "incredibly intelligent" and "detached," someone who showed little emotion, was socially reserved, and had very few online connections. Boy A rejected the suggestion that he tried to influence Girl B. "She didn't have many close friends, did she? But she had you?" Mr. Vance asked.

Question: What did Boy A deny in relation to the events at the park?

A forensic psychological analysis of the Brianna Ghey case, compiled from court documents and evidence, examines the events leading to the fatal stabbing on February 11 in Culcheth Linear Park, Cheshire. The report synthesizes facts: the victim, a transgender teenager, was lured to the park and sustained 28 stab wounds. Two 15-year-olds, referred to in the analysis as Subject X (female) and Subject Y (male), were involved. The analysis notes that a handwritten notebook, recovered from Subject X's residence, contained references to serial killers and was interpreted as indicating a shared fixation with violence. Text communications between the subjects prior to the event were seen as planning the meeting. According to the psychological assessment, Subject X's subsequent statements indicated she was walking away when she heard a scream, turned, and observed Subject Y stabbing the victim approximately five times before fleeing. The analysis highlights Subject X's admission to lying to authorities initially out of fear, and her claimed emotional distress afterward. The findings of an independent review into a major data breach within the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) were published on Monday

A major data breach within the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) has been described as "a wake-up call" for forces across the UK. A report into the data leak has made 37 recommendations for improving information security within the PSNI. In August, the surnames and initials of all the PSNI's 9,500 staff were released by mistake. Police later confirmed that the information was in the hands of dissident republicans, among others. The PSNI and the Policing Board commissioned an independent review of the incident - which was carried out by Pete O'Doherty, temporary commissioner of the City of London Police. His report, which was published on Monday, said the leak was "a wake-up call for every force across the UK to take the security of data as seriously as possible". The PSNI released the information in the form of a vast data spreadsheet, which was attached in error to a Freedom of Information (FoI) request asking for a breakdown of staff roles. It was then published on an FoI website, where it was viewable for two-and-a-half hours before the police had it removed. It included details of where people worked and their roles. Mr O'Doherty's report said the leak was "not the result of a single isolated decision or act by one person, team or department". This sentence summarizes the fundamental reason for the data leak. "At the time of the incident, these factors had not been identified by risk management or scrutiny mechanisms, internal or external." Jon Boutcher described the breach as an "organisational failing"

Current Chief Constable Jon Boutcher said the report "was difficult reading but I accept and indeed embrace the learning within it". "As the report shows, no individual, team, department, decision or act caused this breach - this is an organisational failing, an accumulation of issues," he said. He said every PSNI officer and staff member would be offered a one-off payment of £500 to help with home security measures following the data leak. "Because of the support of the Department of Justice and the Secretary of State, we are able to make that offer," he told a news conference. "It has yet to be finalised. I want to make sure we provide them with the reassurance they deserve. "We need to show them that we support them. "For what is required for most people, it will be sufficient around some cameras and security measures that they would want." "We must take responsibility as a leadership team for this and prioritise information security in our day to day business." The FoI request was answered by the PSNI's human resources department. An individual within the department did not remove a hidden tab containing the spreadsheet of raw data used to compile the FoI response. The tab was visible as three dots, and was also missed by others. Some of the report's recommendations deal with how FoI requests are handled, including file formats. There also needs to be "clarity [as] to who has responsibility for data sign off", it said. The Police Federation for Northern Ireland, which represents rank and file officers, warned it would cost millions of pounds to address the deficiencies which led to the breach. Mr Kelly said given the PSNI already had a significant budget deficit, it would be "impossible for any of these costs to be absorbed by the service, either now or in the future". He said there was an onus on the UK government to allocate funding to implement the report's recommendations. The Catholic Police Guild of Northern Ireland said staff "need and deserve to feel safe" because "nobody should be unable to visit their families, friends and places of worship, especially at this time of year". The PSNI apologised at the time for what was described by senior officers as a "major data breach". It caused considerable concern among PSNI officers and staff, who face a continuing threat from paramilitaries and must be extremely vigilant about their personal security. In September, MPs were told that the breach could cost the service up to £240m in extra security for officers and potential legal action. Mr O'Doherty's report said that following the leak, more than 4,000 PSNI staff contacted the organisation's threat assessment group. One officer "felt it necessary to relocate" and others did so "temporarily", the report revealed. "The review team heard of officers and staff now too frightened to visit friends or family, who have withdrawn from social aspects of their lives and who fear visiting their place of worship," it added. The report described "the potential" for operational consequences for the force as high. "With recruitment and retention already problematic, especially amongst certain communities, this incident is unlikely to provide confidence to those wanting to become part of the service but fearing identification," it added. "There is a risk to the free flow of intelligence, the lifeblood of policing, if those providing it cannot be reassured that they can do this in confidence." The data breach contributed to the resignation of the chief constable at the time, Simon Byrne. He stood down in September, following increasing pressure - with Jon Boutcher subsequently appointed to the role. Earlier on Monday, he said the force had "already taken action" on one of the report's recommendations. "The role of SIRO (Senior Information Risk Owner) has been elevated to the post of deputy chief constable. "This will ensure that information security and data protection matters will be immediately visible to the deputy chief constable, chief operating officer and chief constable, and they can be afforded the support and attention they critically deserve." He added: "The service executive team will now take time to consider the report and the recommendations contained within it. "We will work with the Northern Ireland Policing Board to consider the implications of the report and a timeframe for the completion of relevant actions that have been identified."

The findings of an independent review into a major data breach at the University of North Yorkshire's Student Records System were published on Tuesday.

A significant data breach at the University of North Yorkshire's central administration has been described as "a systemic warning" for higher education institutions nationwide. A report into the data exposure has made 28 recommendations for improving information security within the university's data governance framework. In October, the personal details and academic records of all 12,000 enrolled students were inadvertently disclosed. University officials later confirmed that the information had been accessed by external data brokers and recruitment agencies, among others. The University Council commissioned an independent review of the incident—which was conducted by Dr. Eleanor Vance, interim data protection commissioner for the Higher Education Standards Agency. Her report, published on Tuesday, stated the breach was "a systemic warning for every university in the country to treat student data with the highest level of institutional care." The university released the information in the form of a comprehensive dataset, which was attached in error to a public records request asking for anonymized statistics on student enrollment by department. It was then published on a public research transparency portal, where it remained accessible for three hours before administrators had it removed. It included students' addresses, course enrollments, grades, and disability accommodations. Dr. Vance's report said the exposure was "not the result of a single isolated error by one staff member, office, or software system." This sentence summarizes the fundamental reason for the data breach. "At the time of the incident, these vulnerabilities had not been captured by existing risk assessment or compliance processes, whether internal or external." University Vice-Chancellor Dr. Alistair Finch described the breach as an "institutional governance failure."

Current Vice-Chancellor Dr. Alistair Finch said the report "made for sobering analysis but I accept and intend to implement every lesson identified." "As the report demonstrates, no individual staff member, administrative office, software glitch, or single decision caused this exposure—this is an institutional governance failure, a compounding of systemic gaps," he stated. He said every student affected would be offered a one-time credit of £300 toward identity protection services following the data exposure. "Thanks to the support of the Department for Education and the University Grants Committee, we are able to make that provision," he told a campus press briefing. "The details are still being finalized. I want to ensure we provide the reassurance our student community deserves. We need to demonstrate that we stand with them. For most students, this will cover basic monitoring services and security software they may need." "We must accept responsibility as a senior leadership team for this and prioritize data governance in our daily operational culture." The public records request was processed by the university's Office of Institutional Research. An analyst within that office did not delete a hidden worksheet containing the raw student data used to generate the anonymized statistics. The worksheet was visible as a small tab labeled 'Source,' and its presence was also overlooked by subsequent reviewers. Some of the report's recommendations address how public data requests are managed, including permissible file formats. There also must be "clear delineation of responsibility for final data approval before release," the report stated. The Student Union Association, representing the student body, warned it could cost millions of pounds to remedy the systemic shortcomings that enabled the breach. The Association President noted that given the university's existing budget shortfall, it would be "impossible for these costs to be borne internally, either immediately or in future fiscal cycles." She said there was a clear obligation on the national funding bodies to allocate resources to implement the report's recommendations. The University's Data Ethics Advisory Board stated students "need and deserve to feel secure" because "no student should feel unable to participate fully in campus life, academic societies, or public events, especially during the academic term." The university administration apologized at the time for what senior officials termed a "major failure in data stewardship." It caused significant anxiety among students, who now face increased risks of identity fraud, targeted advertising, and potential discrimination. In November, the Board of Governors was informed that the breach could cost the university up to £180m in enhanced support services, potential regulatory fines, and legal settlements. Dr. Vance's report indicated that following the exposure, more than 3,500 students contacted the university's data protection support unit. One student "felt compelled to change their permanent residence" and others did so "as a temporary precaution," the report noted. "The review team heard from students now too anxious to list the university on their CVs, who have withdrawn from online academic forums, and who fear their data being used for discriminatory profiling," it added. The report assessed "the potential" for academic and reputational damage to the institution as severe. "With student recruitment and retention already challenging, especially from underrepresented backgrounds, this incident is unlikely to inspire confidence in prospective students concerned about privacy," it continued. "There is a risk to the open sharing of academic performance data, essential for learning support, if students cannot be assured their information will be handled confidentially." The data breach contributed to the resignation of the former Vice-Chancellor for Administration, Professor Marcus Reed. He stepped down in November, amid mounting pressure—with Dr. Alistair Finch subsequently appointed to the role. Earlier on Tuesday, he said the administration had "already acted" on one key recommendation. "The role of Senior Data Governance Officer has been elevated to report directly to the Deputy Vice-Chancellor. This will ensure that data security and protection issues are immediately visible to senior leadership and receive the priority attention they critically require." He added: "The University Executive will now dedicate time to reviewing the report and its recommendations. We will work with the University Council to assess the implications and establish a timeline for completing the necessary actions identified."

The PSNI released the information in the form of a vast data spreadsheet, which was attached in error to a Freedom of Information (FoI) request asking for a breakdown of staff roles. It was then published on an FoI website, where it was viewable for two-and-a-half hours before the police had it removed. It included details of where people worked and their roles. Mr O'Doherty's report said the leak was "not the result of a single isolated decision or act by one person, team or department". "It was the consequence of many factors, and fundamentally a result of [the] PSNI not seizing opportunities to better and more proactively secure and protect its data," the report added. "At the time of the incident, these factors had not been identified by risk management or scrutiny mechanisms, internal or external." Jon Boutcher described the breach as an "organisational failing"

Current Chief Constable Jon Boutcher said the report "was difficult reading but I accept and indeed embrace the learning within it". "As the report shows, no individual, team, department, decision or act caused this breach - this is an organisational failing, an accumulation of issues," he said. He said every PSNI officer and staff member would be offered a one-off payment of £500 to help with home security measures following the data leak. "Because of the support of the Department of Justice and the Secretary of State, we are able to make that offer," he told a news conference. "It has yet to be finalised. I want to make sure we provide them with the reassurance they deserve. "We need to show them that we support them. "For what is required for most people, it will be sufficient around some cameras and security measures that they would want." "We must take responsibility as a leadership team for this and prioritise information security in our day to day business." The FoI request was answered by the PSNI's human resources department. An individual within the department did not remove a hidden tab containing the spreadsheet of raw data used to compile the FoI response. The tab was visible as three dots, and was also missed by others. The intended purpose of handling recommendations about FoI requests is discussed here. There also needs to be "clarity [as] to who has responsibility for data sign off", it said. The Police Federation for Northern Ireland, which represents rank and file officers, warned it would cost millions of pounds to address the deficiencies which led to the breach. Mr Kelly said given the PSNI already had a significant budget deficit, it would be "impossible for any of these costs to be absorbed by the service, either now or in the future". He said there was an onus on the UK government to allocate funding to implement the report's recommendations. The Catholic Police Guild of Northern Ireland said staff "need and deserve to feel safe" because "nobody should be unable to visit their families, friends and places of worship, especially at this time of year". The PSNI apologised at the time for what was described by senior officers as a "major data breach". It caused considerable concern among PSNI officers and staff, who face a continuing threat from paramilitaries and must be extremely vigilant about their personal security. In September, MPs were told that the breach could cost the service up to £240m in extra security for officers and potential legal action. Mr O'Doherty's report said that following the leak, more than 4,000 PSNI staff contacted the organisation's threat assessment group. One officer "felt it necessary to relocate" and others did so "temporarily", the report revealed. "The review team heard of officers and staff now too frightened to visit friends or family, who have withdrawn from social aspects of their lives and who fear visiting their place of worship," it added. The report described "the potential" for operational consequences for the force as high. "With recruitment and retention already problematic, especially amongst certain communities, this incident is unlikely to provide confidence to those wanting to become part of the service but fearing identification," it added. Question: How did the prosecutor Allison Hunter KC describe the behavior of the defendants?
samples.modified_input:
The brutal killing of Shakira Spencer has left her cousin Tashica Loo grappling with the horrific reality of what happened. As someone who knew Shakira well, Tashica reflects on the bubbly, kind, and caring person her cousin once was, and how she was slowly isolated and degraded by those she trusted. "For someone who is bubbly and kind and caring, to just be taken away for what? It's heart-breaking," Tashica told the BBC, describing the profound loss.

Shakira's ordeal began when she met Ashana Studholme after becoming neighbors. Studholme, described by authorities as cruel and manipulative, gradually drew Shakira into what was later called a "seedy" social scene, introducing her to drugs and alcohol, which changed Shakira's behavior. Over time, Shakira's relationship broke down, and she became increasingly isolated under Studholme's control, with Studholme eventually taking over her finances and benefits.

The abuse culminated in September 2022 at Studholme's flat in Harrow, where Shakira was subjected to sustained attacks over a weekend. She was beaten, burned with a makeshift blowtorch, and had boiling water poured over her. After being driven back to her own flat in Ealing while dying in a car boot, she was locked in a hall cupboard and later moved to a bunk bed. Her body was left to rot for two weeks before being discovered.

Detective Chief Inspector Brian Howie, who led the homicide investigation, noted Shakira's vulnerability, stating she "just wanted to be cared for, loved, have a friendship group around her and was just coerced and manipulated over a long period of time by these people." He emphasized that the perpetrators showed no remorse and failed to seek medical help when they could have prevented her death.

Ashana Studholme, Lisa Richardson, and Shaun Pendlebury were all convicted of murder and preventing a lawful burial. Studholme had a history of violence, including a racially aggravated assault, while Richardson's flat was known as a hive of anti-social behavior. Pendlebury, who initially confessed to family members before changing his story during the trial, had prior drug offenses.

The case was so harrowing that jurors were excused from service for life. Ealing Council is conducting a Safeguarding Adult Review into the circumstances that led to Shakira's death.

Question: Why did the killers attempt to clean up the crime scene?
samples.modified_input:
Three individuals convicted of the brutal murder of a woman from Manchester were found guilty after a lengthy trial. On Tuesday, October烏, 2023, 32-year-old Maya Patel was transported in a vehicle's rear compartment by individuals she had considered companions. A bystander witnessed her collapse due to severe weakness near the vehicle. This marked the final sighting of her alive. Maya had endured prolonged cruelty from her abusers, who left her body to decompose. Discovery occurred when residents reported insects emerging from beneath her apartment door after ten days. A Manchester Crown Court jury convicted Alisha Khan, Leanne Robertson, and Dean Carter of causing Maya Patel's death and interfering with her lawful burial. Maya Patel had been a vibrant young woman with family and a residence until encountering malevolent influence. She came under the sway of Khan, aged 36, who initially befriended her before exerting control and abuse in the months preceding her death. Khan led the cruel group, which included her associate, Leanne Robertson, 41, and former partner, Dean Carter, 29. Testimony revealed they subjected Maya to prolonged torment, deprivation, burns, and ultimately fatal assaults. Prosecuting attorney James Wilson KC likened them to "a ruthless predatory pack." They treated Maya as a servant, demanding early-morning tasks, limiting her sustenance to condiment packets, while Khan assumed control of her finances. "Maya Patel was dehumanized by these three cruel defendants," Mr. Wilson stated to the jury. Maya Patel gradually succumbed to Alisha Khan's dominance.

Extended abuse culminated horrifically in October 2023 at Alisha Khan's residence in Salford, Greater Manchester, where repeated assaults brought Maya near death. Khan and Carter transported the critically injured woman in a vehicle compartment to her own flat in Bolton, locking her in a storage closet. The perpetrators later returned to relocate her to a lower bunk space. Her vital status at that moment remains unknown. They abandoned her body to decay, undiscovered for ten days. Detective Chief Inspector Mark Evans, leading the investigation, described Maya as susceptible: "She sought care, affection, and social connection but was systematically manipulated over time by these individuals." Maya Patel first encountered Alisha Khan as neighbors. Khan focused on the younger woman, characterized by another neighbor as "a gentle soul, though socially reserved and presenting with cognitive challenges." She drew Maya into what court documents termed her "unsavory" social circle, introducing alcohol and substances that altered Maya's conduct. Maya's familial ties deteriorated, increasing her reliance on Khan, who isolated her progressively. "Alisha Khan is a malicious, controlling personality," DCI Evans noted. "She exhibits a commanding influence over others. She is profoundly corrupt."

In late September, Maya was approached by authorities near Khan's flat due to concerning appearance and behavior. She remained silent and returned to her isolated suffering. Shortly thereafter, Khan messaged Robertson: "I've damaged her severely. Need you now. Risking incarceration." This prompted all three to assemble at Khan's flat. During an October weekend, they executed final sustained attacks on Maya, proving lethal. Scalding liquid was poured on her; a flame combined with aerosol created a torch-like effect, searing her face; she was struck on the head with a weighted device. "They show no regret," DCI Evans observed. "None provided medical aid or summoned professionals when possible. Intervention might have prevented death. Yet, ten days passed before her significantly decomposed remains were located at home."

The impetus for the cleanup effort is provided here. They hurriedly initiated a cleanup operation. Surveillance footage captured them purchasing supplies using Maya's payment card. Khan was recorded exclaiming: "I cannot return to confinement." Their mutual complicity soon fractured. Carter disclosed the group's actions to relatives. His aunt contacted law enforcement. During proceedings, Carter altered his account, denying involvement in Maya's death. At Khan's residence, investigators located documents indicating she received Maya's assistance payments and managed her funds. Some papers were concealed beneath bedding; others in a bag displaying the phrase: "Not my doing." Maya Patel's remains were too degraded for precise cause of death determination. A post-mortem noted extensive injuries to head and feet. Prosecution asserted: "Her body ultimately failed." The cheerful, healthy woman visible in earlier images became emaciated at death. Those familiar with Maya Patel have contemplated her isolation and gradual demise. Her sibling, Rohan Mehta, told media: "For someone so lively and compassionate to be lost for no clear reason is devastating." Khan has a violent record. Jurors learned she assaulted a woman lying in a roadway, resulting in custodial remand. Years earlier, she admitted to a racially motivated assault on another woman. Neighbors of Leanne Robertson in Oldham describe her flat as a center of disruptive activity, with constant visitors and altercations. Dean Carter, whose efforts to dissociate from Maya's killing proved unsuccessful, previously served time for distributing Class A substances. Jurors deliberated extensively before reaching verdicts, released permanently from future service due to the case's distressing nature. Carter gestured sardonically upon murder conviction before exiting. All three await sentencing. Rohan Mehta remarked: "No sentence suffices for their actions. They eliminated a unique individual through abhorrent conduct." Local authorities are conducting a Safeguarding Adult Review.

Mr Milei's inauguration was held in Buenos Aires on Sunday. In a day of pomp and ceremony, the 53-year-old capped his extraordinary rise to power with a speech which left Argentines in no doubt he intends to embark on an economic path unlike any previous president. Mr Milei waved to supporters during a procession to the presidential palace alongside his sister Karina, the confidant who is expected to play an influential role behind the scenes in his new administration. He addressed the crowd and chanted campaign slogans from the balcony, and was presented with the blue and white presidential sash and baton - which he had personalised with engravings of his five dogs. Mr Milei has risen rapidly from relative obscurity to Argentina's highest office on a right-wing platform which includes restricting abortion rights, liberalising gun laws and climate change denial.
